paras: The attempted lynching of Robert L. McNeill was an armed manhunt in Moore County, North Carolina, in May 1888, after McNeill shot Miss Ida Poe at a hotel in Carthage. According to special telegrams from Raleigh, a large party of mounted, armed men searched for him on the night of May 5 and the following days "with the avowed intention of lynching him." McNeill escaped, was reported in South Carolina, and by June was said to have been arrested at Fayetteville and released on bond.

McNeill was the son of A. H. McNeill, clerk of the Moore County Superior Court, and the State Chronicle described him as a young man "of a family of good standing in the county." The Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent called him "a man of bad character" who stood indicted for killing a Black man ("a negro") two years earlier and was out on bail.
Poe, a young woman from Fayetteville, was visiting her brother-in-law, who kept a hotel in Carthage. McNeill had formerly been her admirer, and it was said they had been engaged.

On Saturday evening, May 5, McNeill went to Shaw's Hotel and asked H. A. Foote to tell Poe he wished to see her, but she declined. When she opened the parlor door to a knock, McNeill spoke to her in a low tone and fired a pistol, the ball passing through her thigh near a large artery. He then ran, handing his pistol to a man named Jones while shouting that he had shot her accidentally, and drove off in a waiting buggy. He had reportedly threatened to kill her and Dr. Daniels, a rival who was in the parlor.

A large party of mounted, armed men formed that night and searched for McNeill through Saturday night and Sunday, by the Dispatch's account with the intent to lynch him. Early Sunday "vigilants" went through his father's house, and the three fords of Drowning creek by which he could escape were guarded by armed men. Before daylight on May 8 the town and his father's house were guarded on a rumor that he was hiding there, after a night of searching "with the avowed intention of lynching." By that afternoon the belief was that he had got away toward Texas, though the excitement at Carthage still ran high the next day.

On May 10 McNeill was reported seen near Darlington, South Carolina, and telegrams were sent to the authorities there. The Rockingham Spirit of the South later placed him in Cheraw with his lawyer brother, where no attempt was made to arrest him. In June the Fayetteville Journal reported that he had been arrested in Fayetteville and put under a $400 bond for his appearance at court. Poe's brother reported that her wound was not regarded as dangerous, and no report of a trial for the shooting appears in the coverage.

The first report, a short Raleigh dispatch of May 7, ran in the Washington Evening Star, the Savannah Morning News ("A Tar Heel Town in a Frenzy") and the St. Paul Daily Globe; it spoke of "great indignation" and telegrams for his apprehension but said nothing of lynching. The Richmond Dispatch's special, headlined "Threats of Lynching," was the only account to report an intent to lynch, and its text reappeared on May 16 in a Georgia weekly under an Atlanta Constitution credit with a headline saying he had "Fatally" shot her.

The Dispatch reported the lynching intent without comment, and on May 9 noted that North Carolina was "rather coming towards the front in the matter of lynching." The Raleigh State Chronicle printed its account beside a report of the lynching of Thomas Frazier, which it called "Disgraceful," but did not mention the threat against McNeill; it called him a "jealous rascal" and hoped the law would punish him "to its fullest extent."

Only the Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent reported that the searchers meant to lynch McNeill; the wire report and the State Chronicle described only indignation and efforts to capture him. Early reports said Poe was seriously wounded, while later ones, including her brother's, called the wound painful but not dangerous.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Robert L. McNeill
bases: An armed, mounted party searched for McNeill after he shot Ida Poe, reportedly intending to lynch him, but never caught him (A2, A5).

A 'large party of mounted men' and 'vigilants' hunted McNeill for shooting Poe with the 'avowed intention of lynching him', but he escaped and was later arrested and bonded, so no one was killed (A2, A5, A13).

The shooting and the armed search are reported independently by the Raleigh wire, the Richmond Dispatch special, the State Chronicle and the Raleigh Visitor (A1, A2, A8, A10), though the stated intent to lynch appears only in the Dispatch's Raleigh specials and their reprint (A2, A5, A11).
